newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-MADER AGAIN MISSES GOLD BY A FRACTION.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-MADER AGAIN MISSES GOLD BY A FRACTION.

text.p: A fraction of a second has repeatedly separated Guenther Mader from one of his biggest dreams -- a gold medal.
It happened again on Monday when 0.33 of a second spelt the difference between the Austrian's bronze and Norwegian Atle Skaardal's super-G world title.
"Of course, I would have preferred the gold medal but who wouldn't?" said Mader.
"But I never made a medal in super-G before so I guess it is only normal that one has to start with the smallest medal."

He can put it alongside an illustrious collection of other medals -- four world championship combination bronzes, a 1992 Olympic downhill bronze and a solitary slalom silver from the 1987 world championships.
"I am happier with this super-G bronze than with any of the bronzes from the combination. The combination medals never seem to count for the public," he said.
"Now I finally have a medal in this discipline," said Mader, one of only three skiers to have won World Cup races in all five Alpine disciplines. The others are Pirmin Zurbriggen and Marc Girardelli.

Although Mader has been Austria's most consistent skier since becaming a regular on the circuit in 1983 and has finished second in the overall World Cup standings in 1995 and 1996, his bronze in Sestriere came as something of a surprise.
He was plagued with ankle and back problems shortly before the opening World race in Soelden in October and therefore had a slow start to the season.
He is still chasing his first World Cup race victory of the winter, although he was second in a super-G in Val D'Isere and won a combined in Chamonix last month.

"If I look at what a lousy season I had, then this medal today gains in importance," said Mader. "If your results are good throughout the season then you expect a lot at big events. I was expecting nothing here."
Mader will have at least one other chance to try his luck in Sestriere. He is a medal hope in Thursday's combination and is hoping to race the downhill and giant slalom.
"To make a medal on the first day is a good omen for the rest of the championships," he said jokingly.
Mader, 32, said he would continue skiing while he enjoyed it but that would "probably only be until the (1998) Nagano Olympics.
"Ski racing is a tough sport, it requires a lot of motivation...But it was fun to race here today and that's what counts."
